title: Projection
body:
**Projection is the geometric spine of this course.** Almost every algorithm on the syllabus is
the same move performed somewhere different: drop a vector onto a subspace, keep the shadow,
throw the rest away. [[Least Squares]] is a projection, a coordinate in an
[[Orthonormal Basis]] is a projection, [[Gram-Schmidt]] is repeated projection,
[[Principal Component Analysis]] is a projection onto a subspace chosen to lose the least, and a
[[Fourier Coefficients|Fourier coefficient]] is a projection onto a sine wave.

[[Dot Product]] owns projection onto a single vector. This note owns projection onto
a **subspace** and the matrix that performs it.

## Orthogonal decomposition

Given a subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, every vector splits **uniquely** into a part in $W$
and a part orthogonal to it:

$$
\mathbf{v} = \underbrace{\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{\in\, W} + \underbrace{\mathbf{v} - \hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{\in\, W^\perp}
$$

$\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \text{proj}_W\mathbf{v}$ is the projection and $\mathbf{v} - \hat{\mathbf{v}}$
is the **residual**. Two facts do all the work:

- **The residual is orthogonal to $W$.** This is not a bonus property, it is the definition, and
  every normal-equation derivation in the course is that sentence written in symbols.
- **$\hat{\mathbf{v}}$ is the closest point of $W$ to $\mathbf{v}$.** Any other $\mathbf{w} \in W$
  is further away, by Pythagoras on the right triangle $\mathbf{v}, \hat{\mathbf{v}}, \mathbf{w}$.
  This is the **best approximation theorem**, and it is why "project" and "minimise the error"
  are the same instruction.

Extracting a feature is exactly this: decide which subspace carries the signal, project onto it,
and call what is left noise.

## Computing it

**If you have an [[Orthonormal Basis]] $\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_k\}$ for $W$**, add up
the one-dimensional projections:

$$
\text{proj}_W\mathbf{v} = (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}_1)\mathbf{u}_1 + \cdots + (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}_k)\mathbf{u}_k
$$

One [[Dot Product]] per basis vector. **This formula is false for a non-orthogonal basis**, which
is the single most common error in the course and the reason [[Gram-Schmidt]] exists.

**If you only have a basis as the columns of $A$** ($n \times k$, independent columns), the
orthogonality condition $A^T(\mathbf{v} - A\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}$ rearranges to
$A^TA\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{v}$, so

$$
\hat{\mathbf{v}} = A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{v}, \qquad P = A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T
$$

$P$ is the **projection matrix** for the column space of $A$. Compare it with the
[[Least Squares]] normal equations and you will find they are the same three lines; least
squares *is* this, with $\mathbf{v}$ renamed $\mathbf{y}$.

If the columns are already orthonormal then $A^TA = I$ and it collapses to $P = AA^T$. Do that
whenever possible: no inverse, no conditioning problem.

## Projection matrices

A matrix $P$ is an orthogonal projection exactly when it is both

$$
P^2 = P \quad\text{(idempotent)} \qquad\text{and}\qquad P^T = P \quad\text{(symmetric)}
$$

Idempotent because projecting something already in $W$ changes nothing, so doing it twice is
doing it once. Symmetric because the projection is *orthogonal* rather than skewed along some
other direction.

Consequences worth carrying:

- Its eigenvalues are only $0$ and $1$: fixed on $W$, killed on $W^\perp$. So $P$ is symmetric
  with real eigenvalues and diagonalises orthogonally, by the [[Spectral Theorem]].
- $\text{rank}(P) = \text{tr}(P) = \dim W$.
- $I - P$ projects onto $W^\perp$, and it is the residual-maker.
- $P$ is **not invertible** unless $W$ is everything. It collapses a dimension on purpose, which
  is what [[Determinant|$\det P = 0$]] is telling you and why [[Kernel and Range|rank]] drops.

## Related

- [[Dot Product]]: projection onto one vector, the $k = 1$ case
- [[Orthonormal Basis]] and [[Gram-Schmidt]]: how to get the easy formula
- [[Least Squares]]: the same equations, applied to a system with no solution
- [[Pseudoinverse]]: $P = AA^+$
- [[Principal Component Analysis]]: projection onto the subspace that keeps the most variance
- [[Linear Transformation]] lists projection among the geometric operators
